newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary welcomes U.S. support on NATO entry.
newsitem.headline: Hungary welcomes U.S. support on NATO entry.

text.p: Hungary on Thursday welcomed U.S. support for its entry to NATO alongside Poland and the Czech Republic, and said no country should be ruled out of eventual membership.

"This is a major step," Hungarian foreign ministry spokesman Gabor Szentivanyi told Reuters. "This decision further strengthens us in our expectations that the NATO summit in Madrid will make a favourable decision regarding Hungary's invitation to the alliance."
NATO members are expected to issue formal invitations to new members from former communist Eastern Europe at a summit in Madrid on July 8-9.

"We fully agree with the strong emphasis the (United States) put on leaving the doors open for further new members and that no one should be excluded from consideration for membership," Szentivanyi said.
Defence Secretary William Cohen presented the U.S. position to a meeting of NATO defence ministers in Brussels, their last session before Madrid.

A NATO source at the meeting said the announcement by the alliance's most important member had clearly shocked some other member states. France, in particular, had pushed for a broader enlargement to include Romania and possibly Slovenia.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said in Washington that the U.S. position was firm and other NATO members were unlikely to over-rule it. NATO operates by consensus and the U.S. position is backed by several other countries.
Szentivanyi said that while Hungary felt it should now qualify for the first round of admission, it was in its interest that as many of its neighbours should qualify for membership as possible.

During its long campaign to be considered for early NATO entry, Hungary has concluded basic treaties with all its neighbours ending decades of tension over boundaries and the status of ethnic Hungarians, notably in Slovakia and Romania.

While Slovakia dropped out of contention for early NATO membership after international criticism of its slow rate of reform, Romania has given itself an outside chance of being in the first round since its new reformist government was elected last November.

One of the main priorities of new Romanian president Emil Constantinescu has been to improve relations with Hungary through a string of bilateral accords on military and political cooperation signed earlier this year.
Szentivanyi denied that tensions would appear between Hungary and Romania if Bucharest was left out of the first wave of NATO enlargement.
"I think the relationship (with Romania) is based on firm principles and on a very wide range of economic, political and military exchanges.
"There is trust between the two countries and I believe Hungary will do its best to increase cooperation and through this help Romania's aspirations," he said.
